Former Twilio employee: 'I spent a small time in Segment. The shitty arch is not a point against (micro)services. SendGrid, another Twilio property, uses (micro)services to great effect. Services there were fully independently deployable.'

Commenter on Segment's own engineering blog post: 'I don't think this blog post reflects so well on this engineering team... "We had so many flaky tests that depended on 3rd parties that broke pipelines that we decided on micro-services" is not something I would put on my CV.'

Analysis of Segment's public postmortem: their system used a highly partitioned job database where each partition (event+destination delivery) is handled by at-most-one worker, making a monorepo/monolith a sensible fit for that workload pattern.

One user said they used Twilio SMS and Video, SendGrid, and Segment together before the acquisitions. Now they feel they are 'just sort of using Twilio, Twilio Sendgrid and now Twilio Segment,' as Twilio consolidates enterprise and B2C APIs.

A commenter argued Twilio fits Segment's culture better than Adobe or Salesforce would have, because both rely on developer evangelism to win users. They noted SendGrid, which Twilio acquired earlier, follows a similar strategy.

Critique of Segment's 2018 architecture: having to redeploy 140+ destination services for every shared-library change means Segment had a 'distributed monolith', not real services. A shared library that must stay updated across the whole fleet is antithetical to how services should be treated.

A commenter said Segment's serialization, network-hop and queueing struggles came from poorly defined service boundaries, not from microservices as such. In their view, Segment accidentally built a system with the overhead of distribution but the tight coupling of a single application.

Analysis of Segment's Destinations codebase: per-Destination test suites hit live third-party APIs, so a fast-changing shared library caused spurious failures. Splitting into many repos added version and boilerplate overhead. The commenter called the later move to record/replay tests for each Destination in one repo a 'great move'.

Context from Segment's Centrifuge post: delivery jobs (one event to one destination) live in a highly partitioned job database, with at most one worker per partition. Each worker handles a balanced mix of destinations, so the commenter said consolidating into a monorepo 'makes all the sense in the world.'

Reading Segment's post in hindsight, one commenter felt its problems came less from the micro-vs-monolith trade-off than from the quality and organizational structure of the engineering department. They pointed to the repository and test layout as evidence.
A commenter noted that after Segment's move to a monolith, it still struggles with individual subsystem failures bringing down the whole service.
